title: Care Audit for Home Care Agencies: Six Free Audits to Start With
meta_title: Care Audit for Home Care: Six Free Audits | CareStream
meta_description: Six free audits for home care agencies, from a new care package to a mock inspection. Get started with no card needed and turn every gap into an action.
intro:
A care audit for a home care agency has to work without a building to walk round. Every care audit here starts from the person's records, the visit log and your calls. These six free audits take a domiciliary care agency from a new care package to a mock inspection.

Each audit is free to run on a free CareStream account, with no card needed. Scores are worked out by section, every gap can become an action with an owner and a date, and the registered manager can approve the finished audit. Together the six hold 160 checks.

They are written for registered managers, deputies and care coordinators who audit on paper or in spreadsheets. If you have met audit software that sits behind a trial or charges per user, this page shows what you can run for free. Below the grid you will find what each audit checks, the law behind it and how to get started.
body:
What do six free audits give a home care registered manager?

Six audits will not cover everything an agency does. They do give you a clear path through the parts of a service where problems often start, with a score and an action trail for each.

From a new care package to a mock inspection

The six follow the life of a package. The care package start up and initial assessment audit checks the assessment, risks, consent and early review for one new person. The medication support level audit checks that the help with medicines is recorded and matches the chart.

Next come the care plan and risk assessment audit and the falls and emergency response audit, which also look at one person at a time.

Last come two checks of the whole service. One is the infection prevention and control audit. The other is the mock inspection of the office and a client home.

What each audit checks and how often to run it

Four audits are monthly and look at one person at a time. Two are quarterly and look at the whole service. Pick a different person each month, so the sample grows over the year.

  • Care package start up: 26 checks in 4 sections, monthly.
  • Medication support level and administration: 26 checks in 4 sections, monthly.
  • Care plan and risk assessment: 27 checks in 4 sections, monthly.
  • Falls and emergency response in the home: 25 checks in 4 sections, monthly.
  • Infection prevention and control: 30 checks in 5 sections, quarterly.
  • Mock inspection of office and client home: 26 checks in 5 sections, quarterly.

What each audit records, and what it does not

Each audit records a score for every section, the answer to every check, any photos you add and the signatures. Failed checks become actions that you assign to a named person and track until they are closed.

The audits check records and practice only. They do not hold your rota, record visits as they happen or watch a care worker at a visit. Each audit page says so plainly, so you know what to expect before you start.

Figure: an action plan from a completed audit, with an owner, a due date and a status for each action.

How do these audits fit the duties of a registered provider?

An agency has no corridor to walk or lounge to observe. Your evidence sits in care records, visit logs, staff files and what people and care workers tell you on the phone.

What the law asks of a registered provider

The law sets duties for every provider in England. Regulation 17 on good governance says a provider must have systems to check and improve the quality and safety of the service.

Audits are one way to do that. They are not the only way. A scored audit with signed actions is a record you can show to an inspector, and it shows that checking is part of how the agency runs.

For domiciliary care compliance, that means you can show how you checked, what you found and what you did next. In our view that record matters more than the form it sits on.

Safe care in a person's own home

Four of the six audits sit under safe care and treatment. Regulation 12 says care must be given in a safe way. That includes assessing risks and managing medicines safely.

It also covers preventing and controlling infection. The medication, falls, care plan and infection audits each look at one of these duties as it applies in a person's own home.

They ask for evidence from the person's records, not from memory. A manager who can show the check, the finding and the fix has a stronger story than one who says it was done. Each answer sits beside the person's own file, so a gap is easy to trace.

Practising the five key questions

The Care Quality Commission asks every service five key questions: is care safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. Our mock inspection groups its checks under those headings.

It asks you to sample people and care workers, phone some of them, and visit or observe at least one person's home. It also asks you to check complaints, staff files and earlier audits.

It is a check you run yourself, and it does not predict a rating. Its value is that you find the gaps before anyone else does. Repeat it each quarter with a new sample, so the results build into a trend and you can see whether earlier actions were closed.

Get started free: who it suits and how it compares

Who this is perfect for

This suits a registered manager or deputy of a domiciliary care agency who audits on paper or in spreadsheets. It suits anyone who wants scores, actions and sign off in one place. It also suits a new agency building its first audit routine.

A care coordinator can run the person based audits. A senior who does not manage the records can run the mock inspection. Live in care services can use the medication and falls audits, and should check the other four against how they work.

Our pages on domiciliary care and live in care show how the platform fits each.

Why CareStream is better than the usual alternatives

The usual routes are paper forms, spreadsheets or audit software sold by the user. Paper is quick to start but hard to total, trend or find at inspection. A spreadsheet adds scores but not reminders, signatures or a closed loop on actions.

Many agencies look for audit software and find tools that ask for a trial and a card, or a price for every user. Here every audit is free to run, and the free plan has as many staff logins as you need.

You can upgrade any time and keep everything you have recorded, so starting free costs you no work later. The audits stay the same on every plan.

What the free account includes and what paid plans add

The free account gives you every audit, with reports, signatures and action tracking. You can assign an audit to a named person with a due date, and they are reminded before it is due and when it is overdue.

An overdue audit is escalated to managers. You can also see score trends by month and repeat failures across audits, which helps when you explain to an inspector how a problem was found and fixed.

Paid plans add an action plan drafted for you at the end of an audit. They start at £85 a month after a 14 day free trial, which needs a card. Nothing on this page needs one.

More audits for home care, and where to go next

The library holds more audits for home care than these six. Browse the full library of audits for care services and look for the ones written for the service you run.

Four related collections go deeper. Read about a home care medication audit, a home care safeguarding audit, lone working and safe visits and home care compliance.

Audits find the gaps, and training closes many of them. When a check shows that care workers are unsure, pair the finding with the staff training courses for care workers. Courses on medicines, infection control and moving and handling are good places to look first.

Benefits of CareStream for your home care agency

  • You run six audits free, with no card needed, and see a score for every section.
  • Every failed check becomes an action with an owner and a due date.
  • Your free care audit tool keeps one record of who checked, what they found and who signed it off.

Start with the care package audit on your newest package, and add the others as you go.

faqs.question: What is a care audit for a home care agency?
faqs.answer: It is a structured check of your own records and practice, scored and written down, so you can see what works and what does not. For a domiciliary care agency it samples care plans, visit logs, staff files and calls to people, not a building.

faqs.question: Who should run these audits?
faqs.answer: The registered manager, a deputy or a care coordinator, usually. Each audit page names who it suits. The mock inspection works best when a senior who does not manage the records sampled runs it, so the check is fair.

faqs.question: Are the six audits really free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every audit is free to run on a free CareStream account, with no card needed. The free plan has no end date, and you can upgrade any time and keep everything you have recorded.

faqs.question: How often should a home care agency run them?
faqs.answer: Four of the six are monthly, each looking at one person at a time. The infection prevention and control audit and the mock inspection are quarterly, and each looks at the whole service. Change the pace if your own risks call for it.

faqs.question: Which audit should we run first?
faqs.answer: Start with the care package start up audit on your newest package, because it checks the assessment, risks and consent before problems build. Then add the medicines and care plan audits for the people with the most complex support.

faqs.question: Do these audits cover live-in care?
faqs.answer: The medication support and falls audits are written for home care and live-in care. The other four are written for home care visits, so a live-in service should read each audit page and decide which questions fit.

faqs.question: Does an audit replace our rota or call monitoring system?
faqs.answer: No. These audits check your records and practice. They do not hold your rota, record visits as they happen or monitor calls. Each audit page says what it does not do.

faqs.question: Can I add my own questions or build my own audit?
faqs.answer: Building your own audit, copying one and importing an existing one are Enterprise features. On every plan you can run the library audits as they are and record findings and actions against each question.

faqs.question: Do audits need to be signed off?
faqs.answer: A completed audit can go to the registered manager to approve or send back, with their name, date and signature recorded. We suggest the registered manager signs off every audit so the record shows who reviewed it.

faqs.question: What happens to a failed check?
faqs.answer: Each gap can become an action with an owner, a priority and a due date. The next time you run the same audit, last time's actions are shown so you can check they were closed. Repeat failures show in the trends.

faqs.question: Will running these audits show we meet the regulations?
faqs.answer: No. An audit is evidence that you check your own service and act on what you find. It does not guarantee a rating or an inspection outcome. The Care Quality Commission judges what it sees, hears and reads.

faqs.question: Can several managers or senior staff use the account?
faqs.answer: Yes. The free plan has as many staff logins as you need, so a registered manager, deputy and coordinators can each run and review audits. There is no per user charge on the free plan.

faqs.question: What do paid plans add to the audits?
faqs.answer: An action plan drafted for you at the end of an audit is available on paid plans. Plans start at £85 a month after a 14 day free trial, and the trial needs a card. The audits themselves stay free.

faqs.question: Are there more audits for home care than these six?
faqs.answer: Yes. The library holds more audits for home care, including medicines administration record checks, infection prevention and PPE, complaints and compliments, supervision and competence, and a live-in placement review.

faqs.question: Where do I start if we audit on paper now?
faqs.answer: Pick one person, run the care package start up audit and compare it with your paper form. Create a free account, run the audit on a phone or tablet, and see the score and actions before you change anything else.

title: Home Care Compliance: Six Free Audits for Team and Governance
meta_title: Home Care Compliance: Six Free Team Audits | CareStream
meta_description: Six free audits for home care compliance: recruitment, supervision, spot checks, on call, complaints and review calls. Get started, no card needed.
intro:
Home care compliance rests on proof that your team was recruited safely, supported, observed and listened to. These six free audits turn that proof into scored records, so your home care compliance evidence is ready before anyone asks for it.

Each audit gives every gap an owner and a due date. A manager can then show an inspector what was checked, what was found and what changed, without searching through folders.

The audits are built for domiciliary care agencies, where staff work alone in people's homes and the office rarely sees the care given. Live-in care services can use them too.

If you run audits on paper or in spreadsheets, you can keep doing so. These pages add a set order of checks, a score for each section and a trail of actions that someone owns. You can get started with a free account, and no card is needed at any point.
body:
Free audits that turn team records into governance evidence

Why the team side of governance is where agencies get caught out

Care plans and medicines charts get attention because they are visible. The team records are quieter. A recruitment file with a missing reference, a late supervision or an unlogged out of hours call is easy to miss until someone asks for it.

Regulation 17 on good governance says a provider needs systems to check and improve quality and safety. It also says the provider must keep records about the people it employs.

Every supervision file is part of that evidence. When a manager asks whether a worker was supported, the answer should be a dated record, not a recollection from memory.

How the five key questions point to these records

The Care Quality Commission asks five key questions about every service. The well-led question is about leadership, management and governance, and whether the service encourages learning and an open culture.

That is where recruitment, supervision, complaints and feedback records are read. They show whether leaders know what is happening in the service, and whether they act when something is wrong.

In a visiting service this matters more, because the manager cannot see a shift from the corridor. The records are the only view of the work you have.

The CQC guidance on regulation 17 adds that providers must seek and act on feedback from people using the service, staff and others. A review call that nobody records does not meet that test.

What each of the six audits checks

Each audit is a record check or an observation, scored by section. Every failed check can become an action with an owner and a date.

The recruitment audit follows Regulation 19 on fit and proper persons employed, which says recruitment procedures must be established and operated effectively.

  • Recruitment, DBS and induction of new care workers: 26 checks in 3 sections, from identity, references and Disclosure and Barring Service checks to shadow visits and probation. Run it once for each new starter.
  • Home care supervision, appraisal and competence: 25 checks in 4 sections, covering supervision, observed practice, appraisal and welfare for one worker. Quarterly.
  • Care worker spot check: 44 checks in 7 sections, recorded as you watch an unannounced visit. Quarterly.
  • On call and out of hours response: 25 checks in 4 sections, covering the rota, the call log, response times and handover. Monthly.
  • Home care complaints and compliments: 25 checks in 4 sections, covering the procedure, the response times, learning and praise. Quarterly.
  • Client review call and satisfaction: 28 checks in 4 sections, covering the review schedule, the calls and the survey results. Monthly.

How the six fit together across a month and a quarter

Each month, check the on call line and the review calls. Those two show how the service behaved while you were not watching.

Each quarter, check one worker's supervision, one spot check and the complaints register. Add the recruitment audit whenever someone new finishes probation.

The audits share one pattern, so a manager learns it once. You score each section, then give each gap an action with an owner and a due date. Over several months the scores show whether the same gaps keep returning. That trend is useful evidence in its own right, because it shows learning rather than a single good day.

Who these audits suit, and how they compare

Who this is perfect for

The usual user is a registered manager or deputy at a domiciliary care agency. They run audits on paper or spreadsheets and want a record an inspector can follow. It also suits a field supervisor who carries out spot checks, and a care coordinator who keeps the rota.

If you are searching for domiciliary care compliance tools, remember that no audit replaces your own judgement. These help you gather evidence of it.

Live-in care providers can use the spot check and the review call audit, which are written for live-in care as well as visiting care. Our domiciliary care page shows what else is set up for agencies.

Why CareStream is better than the usual alternatives

The usual alternatives are paper forms, a home made spreadsheet and audit software sold per user. Paper costs little to start but is hard to total. A spreadsheet adds scores, yet nobody chases the actions. Per user software can leave a small agency counting seats.

CareStream puts every audit template on the free plan, with reports, signatures and action tracking. There is no per user fee and no card needed. We also do not claim to replace your judgement.

Fairly, paper and spreadsheets work for many small agencies. Software earns its place when you need scores over time and actions that someone owns.

What the audits do not do

They do not make a service safe, and they do not predict an inspection result. The client review call audit is not survey software. It does not send surveys or make calls. It checks the feedback you already collect, so you still need your own way of asking people.

They also check records and observations, so they depend on honest answers. If a file is missing, the audit shows the gap. It cannot tell you the work was done.

For a wider check across the whole service, the free home care mock inspection audit is the better fit. These six go deeper on the people side.

Get started free, no card needed

What you get on a free account

A free account includes every audit template, with reports, signatures and action tracking. There is no card, no trial clock and no limit on staff logins. Open Audits, pick the audit and name the worker or the month you are checking.

New starters can also take the free Care Certificate course. We do not award the Care Certificate. The employer signs it off after observing practical skills, and the recruitment audit checks Care Certificate progress.

Browse the full care audit library to see what else is available, including audits for medicines charts and infection prevention and control in home care.

Working through two records you already keep

Two of the six audits are about records you already keep. The complaints audit reads your complaints log and a sample of the files behind it. Regulation 16 sets the duty to receive and act on complaints, with a system for recording and responding.

The supervision audit reads one worker's supervision record against your own policy. Staff must get appropriate support, training, supervision and appraisal. A worker who is mostly out on visits still needs a way to be reached. Our supervisions and appraisals tracking feature keeps the dates in one place.

The audit then checks the meeting itself: what was discussed, what was agreed and whether the worker was given a copy.

What paid plans add, and upgrading any time

The free audits stay free. Paid plans add AI recommendations at the end of an audit, written policy checks beyond the first five and training in more than sixty languages. The Starter plan is £85 a month and begins with a 14 day free trial that needs a card.

You can upgrade any time and keep everything you have already done. Nothing on the free plan expires, so you can start with one audit and add others when you are ready.

A written complaints policy is available from the policy shop if you need one. See the complaints policy page for what it covers.

Benefits of CareStream's free audits for home care compliance

  • You get six scored audits for the people side of the service, free, with no card needed.
  • Each gap becomes an action with an owner and a due date, so nothing sits in a folder.
  • Quarterly and monthly repeats show whether the same problems keep returning.
  • You keep your own forms if you prefer them, and use these as a fixed order of checks.

Start with the recruitment audit for your newest care worker, or browse the whole care audit library.

faqs.question: What does home care compliance cover?
faqs.answer: For a home care agency it covers how the service is run as well as the visits themselves. Recruitment checks, supervision, observed practice, the out of hours line, complaints and feedback all sit under it. The six audits here cover that team and governance side.

faqs.question: Do these audits cover every part of domiciliary care?
faqs.answer: No. They cover the team and governance side. Medicines, infection control and care plans need their own audits, and the audit library has free ones for those. These six are the people and leadership evidence.

faqs.question: Who needs to run these audits?
faqs.answer: A registered manager or deputy of a domiciliary care agency, or of a live-in care service, is the usual user. A field supervisor can run the spot check. Anyone who holds the staff files, the rota or the complaints register can complete the matching audit.

faqs.question: How often should each audit be run?
faqs.answer: The audit pages set the frequency. The recruitment, supervision, spot check and complaints audits are quarterly. The on call audit and the client review call audit are monthly. Run the recruitment audit once for each new starter during probation.

faqs.question: Are the audits really free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every audit is free to run on a free account, with no card needed. Reports, signatures and action tracking are included. AI recommendations at the end of an audit are part of the paid plans.

faqs.question: Do I need a card or a trial to get started?
faqs.answer: No. You create a free account and open the audit you want. A card is only asked for when you start a paid plan, which begins with a 14 day free trial.

faqs.question: How long does one audit take?
faqs.answer: It depends on the audit and how ready your records are. Each one has between 25 and 44 checks. Most of the time goes on finding the file, the rota or the register, so keep them to hand before you start.

faqs.question: Can I use my own paper forms instead?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nothing requires software. The audits give you a fixed order of checks, a score and a trail of actions, which a folder of forms does not. You can also build your own audits on the free account.

faqs.question: What is a spot check and how does it differ from supervision?
faqs.answer: A spot check is an unannounced visit where a manager or supervisor watches a care worker in a person's home. Supervision is a meeting about the worker's support and development. The two audits check different evidence, and both feed the picture of a worker.

faqs.question: What should a complaints register hold?
faqs.answer: At a minimum, the date, who complained, what about, who dealt with it, what was found, what was done and when the person was told. The complaints audit checks each of these and also looks for themes and compliments.

faqs.question: How does the on call audit help if nothing went wrong?
faqs.answer: It checks that the rota has no gaps, the call log is complete and decisions and handovers are recorded. A quiet month still tests whether the procedure would work on a bad night.

faqs.question: Will running these audits improve my inspection result?
faqs.answer: We cannot promise any rating or outcome. The audits give you dated evidence that you check your own service, find gaps and act on them. How the Care Quality Commission judges the service is its decision.

faqs.question: What do paid plans add?
faqs.answer: Paid plans add AI recommendations at the end of an audit, written policy checks beyond the first five, and 60 plus languages for training. The Starter plan is £85 a month, and you can upgrade any time and keep everything you have done.

faqs.question: What happens if I stop using CareStream?
faqs.answer: You can stay on the free plan for ever, and nothing forces an upgrade. If you start a paid plan later, you keep everything you have already done.

faqs.question: Do the audits suit live-in care?
faqs.answer: Some do. The spot check and the client review call audit are written for live-in care as well as visiting care. The recruitment, supervision, on call and complaints audits are written for home care agencies, and the questions still apply to a live-in service.

title: Lone Working Risk Assessment Audits for Home Care, Free to Run
meta_title: Lone Working Risk Assessment Audits for Home Care | CareStream
meta_description: Six free audits for home care: check a lone working risk assessment, key safe access, home risks, handling, rotas and missed visits. No card needed.
intro:
A lone working risk assessment helps only if it matches the round: the door that will not open, the late call, the long drive home. This collection gives you six free audits, so you can check a lone working risk assessment against real visits and not only a signed form.

The audits follow a care worker through the day. One covers getting in, three cover staying safe, and two look at whether every visit gets done. Each audit scores its checks and turns every gap into an action with an owner and a date. You see what was checked, what was found and who is fixing it.

This page is for the registered manager or deputy of a domiciliary care agency who runs audits on paper or in spreadsheets. It is also for live-in care providers who want the same checks without extra cost. You can get started on a free CareStream account with no card needed.
body:
How do six free audits protect a care worker from front door to last visit?

A care worker on a round has no colleague in the room. The risks arrive in order: getting in, being in the home, then keeping to the rota. The six audits follow that order.

Getting in: key safes, codes and what happens when no one answers

The first risk is the door. The key safe, access and no reply audit runs quarterly across the service, using a sample of people. Its 27 checks sit in four sections: access arrangements, keys and codes, the no reply procedure, and review and learning.

It asks whether the way in was agreed with the person, where each code is kept and who can see it.

It then samples real no reply events to see what the care worker did next. It checks your records and does not hold or issue codes. Each gap, such as a code never changed after a person moved on, becomes an action with a named owner.

Staying safe: the worker, the home and moving people

The lone working audit is run quarterly for one care worker at a time. It has 39 checks in six sections, from the risk assessment to check in and escalation, travel, personal safety, training and kit, and incident follow up. You can read the lone working and care worker safety audit in full before you sign up.

The home environment and client risk audit looks at the place itself, with 44 checks in seven sections. It covers access, fire, gas and electrics, equipment, pets, smoking and oxygen.

The moving and handling in the home audit checks one client each quarter, with 43 checks, including observed practice and two person tasks.

Getting every visit done: rota, travel time and late or missed visits

A safe worker still fails the person if the visit does not happen. The rota, continuity and travel time audit is monthly and covers the whole service. Its 28 checks look at travel time between calls, round design, the same care workers visiting the same people, short notice changes and cover.

The late and missed visit review is also monthly. Its 44 checks follow the month from the visit log to the reasons, the pattern by round, what people told you and how your alerts work. Put the two together and you can trace late calls back to the rota that caused them.

What does each audit record, and what do the six not do?

Each audit produces a score, a list of findings and a log of actions. It does not write your documents for you.

How the audits work from first check to action log

Each audit is a set of scored checks in named sections. You answer from your own records: the care plan, the rota, the visit log, the worker file. Where something is missing you add a finding.

Every finding becomes an action with an owner and a due date. The next run shows whether the same gap is still open.

The schedule differs across the six. Key safe, lone working and moving and handling are quarterly. Rota and late and missed visits are monthly. The home audit runs at the start of care and at every review, so each person's home is checked when it matters.

What the audits do not do

These audits check; they do not replace anything you own. They do not write your risk assessments for you, issue key safe codes, track a worker's location or record visits as they happen. Your rota system and call monitoring do that work.

They also do not say your service is safe. The registered manager still decides what to do with each finding.

We suggest keeping each completed audit with its action log. That way you can show an inspector what was found, who took the action and what changed afterwards. A short note on why a gap was accepted, where it was, belongs there too.

What the law and guidance expect of the employer

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) says lone workers face the same hazards as anyone else, with a greater risk of harm. There may be no one to help. It adds that employers should provide training, supervision, monitoring and support.

Lone worker risk starts with the assessment. The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 apply. Regulation 3 on risk assessment says an employer must assess the risks to employees at work.

For people receiving care, the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 apply. Regulation 12 on safe care and treatment says care must be provided in a safe way. The registered person must assess risks and reduce them as far as is reasonably practicable.

Staffing is covered by Regulation 18 on suitably skilled staff and their support. Staff must receive the support, training and supervision they need to do their work.

The HSE topic pages on working alone offer advice for employers and for lone workers themselves. Read the HSE lone working advice beside the lone working audit, then look at the lone worker guidelines in your own policy.

Who is this free set of audits for, and how does it compare with the usual routes?

Who this is perfect for

This set is for registered managers, deputies and field supervisors of domiciliary care agencies. Care coordinators and schedulers will use the rota and visit audits most. Live-in care providers can use the lone working, home, handling and visit audits, which list live-in care among the services they suit.

It also suits supported living and Shared Lives services for the lone working audit.

The key safe and rota audits are written for domiciliary care rounds. If you audit with a paper form and a spreadsheet of dates, these give you the same checks with scores and actions in one place. Nobody has to retype a finding from the form into the tracker.

Why CareStream is better than the usual alternatives

The usual routes are a paper audit file, a spreadsheet you maintain yourself, or audit tools sold per user after a trial. Paper and spreadsheets are free but hold no scores or action trail. Paid software gives you a tracker, but you pay for it before you know it fits.

You get every audit free, with no card needed and as many staff logins as you need. Completed audits, scores and actions stay on your account. If you outgrow it, you can upgrade any time and keep everything you have recorded.

Compare it on one question: could a care coordinator open last quarter's audit, see which action is still open and who owns it? That is what the free account is built to show.

Related policy, training and audit pages

The audits work best beside your own documents. The lone working policy for care services sets out the rules the audit checks against. The lone working awareness course for care teams is the training that the audit asks about.

If you want the training and policy side in one place, see our collection of lone working training for community care staff. The full list of audits is on the care audits index.

Using them together makes the picture whole. The policy states the rule, the course teaches it, and the audit shows whether it is followed on a real round. A gap in any one of the three usually shows up first in the audit findings.

Get started with the free audits, no card needed

What to run first

Sign up for a free account, then choose one care worker for the lone working audit. Pick someone who covers a rural round or works long evening calls. Run it from their file and a short conversation with them. Ask what happens at a check in that is missed, and write down their answer in their words.

In the same week, run the late and missed visit review for last month. Together they show whether your people are safe and whether visits are happening. Then add the key safe, home and handling audits as your quarter allows. Give each action an owner before you close the audit, so the next run has something to measure against.

Upgrade any time

All six audits stay free. A paid plan adds AI recommendations at the end of an audit and starts with a 14 day trial that needs a card. Starter is £85 a month, Professional is £230 and Enterprise is £385. Choose a paid plan only if the extras matter to you.

If you stop a paid plan, your recorded audits stay on your free account. Nothing you have recorded is held back, and the six audits remain free to run for as long as you want them.

intro:
A MAR chart is the record of every medicine a person is given at home, so checking it sits at the heart of a home care medicines audit. Does the MAR chart show help that was assessed, written down and followed on each visit? Whether you work from paper or a screen, the aim is the same: find the gap before it reaches the person.

This page brings together six free audits for domiciliary care agencies and live-in care. They cover the level of support, the record, carer competence, self-administration, and the daily and weekly checks. Each scores your answers and turns every gap into an action with an owner and a date.

You run them on a free account with no card needed, with as many staff logins as you need. We wrote this for registered managers and deputies who audit on paper or in spreadsheets. They may have met audit software behind a trial or a per user charge. Read on to see what each audit checks.
body:
What a home care medicines check has to cover

Why a person's own home changes the audit

A care home keeps its medicines in one place under one team. A domiciliary care agency does not. The medicines sit in the person's home, supplied by their pharmacy, and different carers arrive on different visits.

Between visits, the written record is often the only evidence of what happened. That is why we split these audits by question rather than by room.

One asks what level of help the person needs. Another asks whether the record matches it. A third asks whether the carer was competent to give it.

Live-in care adds a carer who may work alone for days, so nobody else sees the round. Our pages on policy access for domiciliary care agencies and tools for live-in carers on their own phone show how the platform supports them.

What the law and NICE guidance ask of a registered manager

The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspects registered providers. The rules it uses are in the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014.

One of them is Regulation 12 on safe care and treatment says medicines must be managed properly and safely.

Regulation 17 covers good governance. It asks providers to assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the service. A regular audit of how medicines are managed is one way to show that you do this.

The same regulation covers staff. The CQC guidance on regulation 12 says staff need the competence, skills and experience to keep people safe.

NICE has a guideline for this setting, NG67 on managing medicines for adults receiving social care in the community. It covers assessing support needs, staff competency and record keeping. In our view it is worth reading beside any audit.

Where electronic records fit

Many agencies now use an electronic MAR chart inside their care software. Others work from a MAR chart template printed by the pharmacy. MAR means medication administration record. The audit questions work with either, because you open the record and answer each check.

In our view, the useful question is not which system you use. It is whether the check finds what the record hides. A signature on a screen can still sit beside a missed dose, and a gap on paper may be explained by the notes.

These audits do not import your record or replace your care software. They keep a scored record of your check, with actions attached.

For a worked example of a medicines round and the recording errors to avoid, read our guide to completing a medicines administration record.

Our plain guide to how a medication audit works covers the wider routine.

The six free audits and who each one suits

The record check and the support level check

The first is the medication support level and administration audit. It covers one person at a time, with 26 checks in four sections. It asks whether carers prompt, assist or administer, and whether the plan, the record, the pharmacy supply and the visits all agree.

We set it to monthly. It is written for home care and live-in care.

The second is the chart audit for home care. It has 42 checks in seven sections and follows one person's completed chart: signatures, codes, missed doses, allergies, as needed medicines and creams. It also checks the chart against the care plan and daily notes.

Run the first to see whether the arrangement is right. Run the second to see whether the record proves it. In our view, rotate the person each month so every chart is checked over a few months.

Competence and self-administration

The competence assessment for medicines is for one care worker at a time. It has 41 checks in six sections, from training and knowledge to observed practice and sign off.

We suggest using it at induction, each year and after a medicines error. Medication competency means a carer shows safe knowledge and practice. The assessor should be trained to assess medicines competence.

The self-administration of medicines audit checks one person who looks after some or all of their own medicines. It has 41 checks in six sections and is set to quarterly.

Its listed services do not include home care. They are care homes, supported living, extra care, Shared Lives and similar. For a person in their own home, read the questions first and judge whether they fit.

The daily check and the weekly stock check

These two are written for services that keep medicines on site. The daily check covers the whole service over the last 24 hours, with 20 checks in five sections. Its listed services do not include home care.

The weekly stock and storage check has 11 checks in three sections: storage, controlled drugs and stock. It is a walk round a medicines room, which most agencies do not have.

We include both for honesty, not to stretch the page. A domiciliary agency will get more from the monthly checks. A provider that also runs extra care or supported living with medicines on site can use the daily and weekly checks there.

Who this is perfect for, and how it compares

Who this is perfect for

It suits the registered manager or deputy of a home care agency who checks medicines on paper or in a spreadsheet. It also suits the nominated individual. They can see in one place who has been checked, and when.

It also helps a provider of live-in care, where one carer is responsible for every dose and the record carries the weight. Supported living and extra care providers can use the same checks for people they support.

It is less suited to a service that wants the audit to read its electronic records and score them without a person. These audits depend on someone opening the record and answering honestly.

Why CareStream is better than paper, spreadsheets and gated software

Paper and spreadsheets cost nothing, but they leave you counting by hand. Nobody sees a trend across people and months, and an action with no owner is easy to lose. Many audit tools add the opposite problem: a trial first, then a charge per user.

Those tools may offer more elsewhere, and a spreadsheet you built yourself may fit your agency well. We claim only this: the scored audit, the finding, the action and the trend are all free to use.

CareStream gives you each of those on the free plan, with no card needed. We say better only for the points above.

Get started free with no card needed

What the free account includes

The free plan includes every audit template, 30 in all, with reports, signatures and action tracking. It also includes CPD certified training for staff and as many staff logins as you need. Create a free account on the free care audits page and pick an audit.

Each completed audit gives a score for every section, a list of findings and the actions with their owners and dates. Reports and signatures are included, so you can show an inspector what you checked and what you did next.

Paid plans add AI recommendations at the end of an audit. They start with a 14 day free trial that needs a card. If you upgrade, you keep everything you recorded.

Running the first month

Start with the support level audit for one person who has a mix of prompted and given medicines. Then run the record audit for another person. Give every gap an owner and a date, so nothing is left as a note.

Add the competence assessment for any carer you have not watched give medicines. The care worker spot check records an unannounced visit, including medicines.

Where an audit finds a knowledge gap, the medication support in the community training is there for community care staff. An audit does not decide a rating or an inspection outcome. It shows that you looked, and what you did next.

Benefits of CareStream for a home care medicines audit

  • Six free audits cover the level of help, the MAR chart, competence, self-administration, and daily and weekly stock.
  • Each audit scores your answers and turns gaps into actions with an owner and a date.
  • The free plan has no card, no per user charge and no end date.
  • We say which audits fit home care and which do not.

faqs.question: What is a medicines audit in home care?
faqs.answer: It is a regular, recorded check that the help a person gets with medicines was assessed, is written down and is followed on visits. In home care it usually looks at one person at a time, using their care plan, their administration record and the notes from visits.

faqs.question: Who should carry out a medicines audit in a domiciliary care agency?
faqs.answer: Usually the registered manager, the deputy or a senior care worker trained in medicines. Whoever does it should be able to read the administration record, compare it with the care plan and judge whether a gap matters. The audit pages name who runs each one.

faqs.question: How often should medicines be audited in home care?

faqs.question: What is the difference between prompting, assisting and administering?
faqs.answer: When prompting, a carer reminds the person and the person takes their own medicines. When administering, the carer gives the medicine. The support level audit checks that the care plan, the administration record and the visits all agree on which level applies.

faqs.question: Do these audits replace my care software or my pharmacy chart?

faqs.answer: Not as written. It covers the whole service over the last 24 hours and its listed services do not include home care. An agency is better served by the monthly checks on one person at a time. A service that keeps medicines on site, such as extra care, can use it.

title: Home Care Safeguarding Checklist: Six Free Audits for Consent, Money and Injuries
meta_title: Home Care Safeguarding Checklist: Six Free Audits | CareStream
meta_description: Use a safeguarding checklist for home care, free. Six audits cover consent, skin, money, injuries and candour, with actions tracked. No card needed.
intro:
A safeguarding checklist for a home care agency has to look past the log. In our experience, concerns about abuse often start as a missing consent form, a gift nobody recorded or a bruise that was never charted. A good safeguarding checklist follows those threads, and this collection groups six free audits that do.

Each audit scores a set of checks and turns every gap into an action with an owner and a due date. Some run monthly and some quarterly, and your results build into a trend for each one. All six are free on a free account, with no card needed and no limit on staff logins.

This page is for registered managers and deputies of domiciliary care agencies, and for live-in care managers, who audit on paper or in spreadsheets today. It says plainly what each audit checks, how often to run it, and what none of them can do.
body:
Six free audits for safeguarding, consent and capacity at home

Care workers visit one person at a time and often work alone. Safeguarding records therefore sit in several places: the care plan, the daily notes, the money record and the incident log. Reviewing only one of them leaves the rest unchecked.

What each of the six audits checks

The safeguarding log review is the closest match to a monthly check of the log. It has 10 checks in 2 sections and starts from the log you already keep. It checks that each concern was logged, referred, notified and shared with the person, then looks at themes and staff training.

The client money, shopping and gifts audit has 28 checks in 4 sections. It follows the care plan, the money record, receipts, cash counts and the gifts record, then any concerns raised.

The injury recording audit has 28 checks in 4 sections. It looks at the body map template in use at the start of care and at how each entry is written. It also checks that a mark reached the safeguarding lead the same day.

Skin care, capacity, consent and candour

The mental capacity and consent in the home audit has 28 checks in 4 sections. You audit one person at a time, using their signed agreements, capacity assessments, best interests records and any attorney papers. It also checks restrictions on their freedom at home.

The duty of candour audit has 41 checks in 6 sections. It covers a whole quarter of incidents. Each notifiable incident is tested against the evidence. That means the notification, the conversation, the apology and the letter.

The pressure area and skin care in the home audit has 28 checks in 5 sections. You audit one person at a time, using their skin risk assessment, care plan, daily notes, and equipment records. It checks skin checks on visits, equipment in the home and nurse escalation.

How often to run each audit

The log review, the pressure area audit, the money audit and the injury audit are monthly checks. The capacity audit for the home and the duty of candour audit are quarterly.

Those intervals come from the audits themselves. They are our suggested practice, not a rule in law. A larger agency may audit a sample of people each month, while a small one covers everyone.

Pick the pattern you can keep. The same checks at the same time each month show more than one big audit a year. Put the dates in the diary, give each audit an owner, and let the deputy cover when the manager is away.

What the six audits do not cover

The collection has limits, and we would rather state them than stretch them.

What the skin care audit does and does not do

The pressure area and skin care audit is run monthly for one person at a time. It checks the records and the home. It does not replace a nurse's assessment, and it does not score a risk assessment tool for you. It does not check consent either, so pair it with the capacity audit for the home.

It pairs with the injury recording audit. Skin damage can come from missed visits, short visits or poor care. The audit checks that this was recorded and passed to the manager, who decides whether to tell the safeguarding lead. A nurse is told the same day, so the audit also checks who was told and when.

What an audit cannot do

None of the six decides whether anyone has been harmed. The money audit records what you find and passes concerns to your safeguarding lead. The injury recording audit and the skin care audit record the mark and escalate it.

The decision stays with your safeguarding process and the local authority. Under section 42 of the Care Act 2014, the council makes enquiries when it suspects an adult with care needs is at risk of abuse or neglect.

An audit supports that route and does not replace it. Nor does any audit promise an inspection rating. It shows what you checked and what you did about it.

Why safeguarding in home care needs these records

The duties behind these audits sit in the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014. Several of them meet in a person's own home, where nobody else is watching.

Consent and capacity in the person's own home

Consent in care at home starts with regulation 11. Care and treatment can only be provided with the consent of the relevant person. Where a person aged 16 or over cannot consent because they lack capacity, the provider must follow the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

That Act begins with a set of principles. A person is assumed to have capacity unless it is shown they lack it. An unwise decision does not prove they lack it.

In a person's home, relatives, attorneys and care workers all make everyday decisions. The audit checks that the record shows whose decision it was, and about what. It also checks that capacity was assessed for one decision at a time, not for the person as a whole.

Money, gifts and shopping

Regulation 13 protects people from abuse. It counts theft or misuse of a person's money or property as abuse.

That is why receipts and gift records belong in a safeguarding review. A care worker who buys groceries or is offered a gift needs a clear record behind them.

The money audit checks what the care plan allows and who has authority. It checks that receipts and cash counts agree. It also checks what happened when something looked wrong.

The Care Quality Commission also publishes its guidance on regulation 13, which explains the intent behind the rule.

We suggest writing the arrangement into the care plan before the first shop, not after a worry has been raised.

Injuries, candour and notifications

Care workers may be the only people who see a mark on someone's skin. If it is not recorded on the first day, nobody can show later whether it was new. An unexplained or worsening skin change can also be a sign of neglect, so it must reach a nurse and the safeguarding lead.

Regulation 20 sets the duty of candour. After a notifiable safety incident, the provider must tell the person concerned face to face, with an apology, and then write to them.

The injury audit tests the first step, the report to the safeguarding lead. The candour audit tests the follow up, from the conversation to the letter and the notification to the Care Quality Commission.

Our guide to running a safeguarding audit in a care service shows how the log review fits with these two.

Who this suits and how it compares with other options

Who this is perfect for

This collection suits a registered manager or deputy of a domiciliary care agency. They run monthly audits on paper or in a spreadsheet and have to show governance. It also suits live-in care providers, where one care worker may be the only person who sees a mark or a receipt.

It suits a safeguarding lead who wants one place for concerns, injuries, money checks and candour follow up. Supported living services can use the same audits for the people they support. A nominated individual can read the scores without sitting in on each audit.

For the written side, see the safeguarding policies collection for care services.

Why this is a better fit than the usual alternatives

The usual routes are a spreadsheet kept by the deputy, a paper audit pack, or audit software priced per user with the useful features behind a trial. A spreadsheet is quick to start but hard to share and sign. Paper is quick to complete, though actions get lost.

Here all six audits sit on the free plan. There is no card, no trial clock and no charge per user, because the plan includes as many staff logins as you need. Scores, signatures and action tracking are part of the free plan.

Paid plans add recommendations at the end of an audit, and we say so openly. You compare plans only if you want those extras.

Get started free, with no card needed

Sign up for a free CareStream account and open the audits. Pick the log review first, as it has only 10 checks and starts from a log you already keep.

Then add the injury, skin care and money audits each month. Put the capacity and candour audits in the diary each quarter. Every free audit is listed on the care audits page, so you can add others later.

Safeguarding training sits alongside the audits and gives staff the knowledge the audits test. The safeguarding adults and children course for care staff fits well, because the log review looks at what staff know.

Benefits of CareStream's free audits for a home care safeguarding checklist

  • You run the log review, skin care, money, injury, capacity and candour audits without a card.
  • Every gap becomes an action with an owner and a due date.
  • Scores build into a trend, so you can show governance over time.
  • As many staff logins as you need are included on the free plan.

Start with the log review this month, and read the results before you decide anything else. CareStream keeps what you record when you upgrade.
